evidence.label: Interior regularity of planar Mumford–Shah minimizers

headline: Claims interior Mumford–Shah regularity in the plane: edges are smooth arcs, crack tips or 120-degree triple junctions.
scope: Reduced absolute minimizers of the planar Mumford–Shah energy in a bounded Lipschitz domain, with bounded measurable data, away from the domain's boundary.
plain: The Mumford–Shah problem cleans up a picture by finding a smooth image plus a set of edges where it may jump. Long edges cost energy, so the best edge set should be simple. Mumford and Shah conjectured that, inside the picture, it is made of smooth curves, curve ends and three-way junctions at 120 degrees. This paper claims to prove that interior statement in the plane. It also claims only finitely many separate pieces of the edge set meet any region away from the boundary.
doesNot: This does not cover what happens at the boundary of the domain, or dimensions above two. It has no Lean check, and a separate recent preprint by Deangelis claims a proof by another route.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: David Mumford and Jayant Shah, a variational model for image segmentation
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims the interior regularity part of a well-known conjecture in the calculus of variations, with a new compact-piece argument.

explanation:
Draw a crack along the negative x-axis in the plane, ending at the origin. Away from the crack, let u = √r sin(θ/2), where r is the distance to the origin and θ is the angle. This function jumps across the crack and is smooth elsewhere. Its slope has size 1/(2√r), which blows up at the tip. The slope is bigger than t only where r < 1/(4t²). For t = 10 that is r < 0.0025, a disc of area about 0.0000196. In general that area is π/(16t⁴), so it shrinks like t⁻⁴. Mathematicians call this weak L⁴. This crack tip is one of the shapes the theory expects.

The Mumford–Shah energy scores a pair: a function u and a closed set K where u may jump. It adds the squared slope of u off K, the length of K, and the squared distance from given data g[2]. Mumford and Shah proposed it to split an image into regions[3]. Their conjecture predicts that, inside the domain, K is made of smooth arcs with only free ends and triple junctions[4]. Bonnet, David, Ambrosio, Fusco and Pallara built most of the regularity theory. After their classification results, one obstacle remained for blow-up limits: a possible bounded piece of the limiting edge set[5].

The paper claims the interior part of the conjecture for reduced absolute minimizers with bounded data. Near every point of K, the set is a smooth arc through the point, an arc ending there, or three arcs meeting at 120 degrees[1]. Only finitely many connected pieces of K meet any region kept away from the boundary[6]. It also deduces that the slope of u is weak L⁴ near each interior point, matching the crack tip above[7].

The key step rules out the bounded piece. Moving that piece sideways keeps its length the same[8]. An interaction energy then depends on the shift in a harmonic way, and minimality forces it to be constant. This makes the remaining fields zero, so deleting the piece saves length, a contradiction[9]. A recent preprint by Deangelis also claims the classification and the interior structure, by a different argument[10].

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The proof relies on a large body of earlier regularity theory, used as stated in the literature. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds: it would settle the interior part of the planar Mumford–Shah conjecture. Another recent preprint claims the same by a different route. There is no Lean check or published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: A score for an image and its edges: slope off the edges, plus edge length, plus distance from the data.
A pair whose energy cannot be lowered by any change confined to a compact region inside the domain.
With no useless bits of zero length added to the edge set.
A point where an edge curve simply stops.
A point where three edge curves meet, here at equal 120-degree angles.
A size condition: the area where the slope exceeds t is at most a constant times t⁻⁴.
The shape seen by zooming in on a point more and more closely.
